questions.prompt: An LLM answers a question about a vendor contract it was never trained on with a specific, confident-sounding number anyway. Based on how hallucination actually works mechanically, why doesn't the model instead say it doesn't know?
options: Because it's a next-token predictor with no built-in signal distinguishing "confident because I know this" from "confident because that's what plausible text looks like" — it keeps predicting plausible tokens regardless
Because the model secretly knows the answer is wrong but is instructed to never admit uncertainty
Because every LLM is hard-coded to always answer in a confident tone regardless of the question type
Because the model first checks the internet for the real contract and only guesses if the lookup fails
questions.explain: A hallucination isn't a glitch — it's the predictable output of next-token prediction. When the true answer isn't in the model's training data, it has no fallback mode that signals uncertainty; it just keeps producing the statistically plausible continuation, which reads exactly as confidently as a correct answer.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the RAG query-time loop, from Lesson 3, in the order a query actually goes through them.
items: The user asks a question in plain text
The question is embedded using the same embedding model used on the documents
The vector database retrieves the top-k chunks closest to the query vector
The retrieved chunks and the original question are assembled into a prompt
The LLM generates an answer grounded in the retrieved text
questions.explain: Lesson 3's query-time loop runs in exactly this order: embed the query with the ingestion-time model, retrieve the closest chunks, assemble them with the question into a prompt, and only then generate — each step depends on the one before it.

questions.prompt: Select every situation below where, according to Lesson 4, standing up a full RAG pipeline is probably the wrong call.
options: The entire knowledge base is one short policy document that would fit directly inside the model's context window
The goal is to make the model consistently write in a specific brand voice, not know new facts
The question needs an exact computed value, like today's live exchange rate
The knowledge base is large, updated weekly, and every answer needs to cite which document it came from
The knowledge base is a handful of FAQ answers that almost never change
questions.explain: Lesson 4 names four cases where RAG adds complexity without value: the knowledge fits in the prompt anyway, the task is really about style, the knowledge is static and small, or the task needs computation rather than retrieval. A large, frequently changing, citable knowledge base is the opposite case — that's exactly where RAG earns its cost.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ continues training an existing model on your own examples and adjusts its weights directly, while RAG leaves the model's weights untouched and retrieves relevant text into the prompt at query time instead.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 draws this exact line: fine-tuning bakes knowledge or behavior into the model's weights through further training, while RAG keeps the weights frozen and supplies knowledge externally, at query time, from a store you can update without retraining anything.

questions.prompt: What is a text embedding, as produced by an embedding model?
options: A dense numeric vector representing a piece of text's meaning as a point in high-dimensional space, trained so that similar meanings land near each other
A compressed, losslessly reversible copy of the original text
A sparse, mostly-zero vector built purely from exact word counts
A hash used only to detect exact duplicate documents
A keyword index mapping each word to the documents containing it
A checksum used to verify a file wasn't corrupted in transit
questions.explain: An embedding is a dense numeric vector produced by a neural network trained so that text with similar meaning lands at nearby points in vector space — distance and direction become a proxy for semantic similarity.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes an old-style bag-of-words vector, which Lesson 5 explicitly contrasts with a real embedding — bag-of-words is mostly zeros and encodes only word counts, while a dense embedding has almost every value non-zero and learned to represent meaning, not vocabulary.

questions.prompt: A vector from OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small and a vector from an open-source BGE model are both exactly 1536 numbers long. Why can't they still be compared to each other with cosine similarity?
options: Each model's embedding space is defined entirely by its own training — architecture, data, objective — so same-length vectors from two different models place concepts at incomparable coordinates
Cosine similarity mathematically requires both vectors to come from the same API provider
1536-dimension vectors can only be compared if they were generated less than 24 hours apart
Open-source models always output vectors in a different numeric format that can't be compared at all
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit: an embedding space is entirely defined by how its specific model was trained. Two models that happen to output vectors of the same length still place concepts at completely different coordinates, so comparing them produces a meaningless score.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 walks through this by hand: cosine similarity divides the raw dot product by both vectors' magnitudes, which is exactly what turns an otherwise unbounded number into a comparable score between -1 and 1 regardless of vector length.

questions.prompt: Match each similarity/distance concept to how it actually behaves.
right: Measures the angle between two vectors, ranging -1 to 1, ignoring magnitude
Sum of the products of matching vector components; also affected by magnitude
Straight-line distance between two points, where lower means more similar
Rescaling a vector to length 1, after which dot product and cosine similarity agree
questions.explain: Lesson 7 covers all three metrics plus the normalization trick that unifies two of them: cosine ignores magnitude entirely, dot product doesn't, Euclidean distance works in the opposite direction (lower is more similar), and L2-normalizing every vector to length 1 is exactly what makes dot product and cosine similarity produce identical rankings.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about embedding dimensionality trade-offs.
options: Storage cost per vector is dimensions × 4 bytes, for vectors stored as 32-bit floats
A lower-dimensional embedding is always the better choice because comparisons are cheaper
Matryoshka Representation Learning lets you truncate a vector's first N dimensions and still get a coherent, usable embedding without re-running the model
Comparing two 3072-dimension vectors takes roughly twice the compute of comparing two 1536-dimension vectors
The right dimensionality is whichever one is largest, regardless of what evaluation on real retrieval quality shows
questions.explain: Lesson 8 frames this as a real trade-off, not a race to the smallest or largest number: storage scales as dimensions × 4 bytes, compute scales with dimension count, MRL lets you truncate a vector and still get a usable embedding, and the right size is the smallest one that still gives acceptable retrieval quality for your content — not simply the smallest or the largest available.

questions.prompt: What is the core operation a vector database is purpose-built to answer quickly?
options: Approximate nearest-neighbor search: which stored vectors are closest to a given query vector
Exact-match and range queries over structured columns, like a relational database
Enforcing foreign-key constraints between related tables
Computing aggregate functions such as SUM and AVG across stored rows
Full-text keyword search, entirely independent of any vector math
Running scheduled backups of structured transactional data
questions.explain: Lesson 10 draws a direct contrast: a relational database is built around exact matches and range queries over structured columns, while a vector database is built around approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search — finding the most similar vectors by distance, not an exact match.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a relational database's core operation, not a vector database's. A vector database deliberately trades exactness for speed via approximate nearest-neighbor search, which is a fundamentally different kind of query than an exact WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: An IVF index has nlist=2,000 clusters over 4,000,000 vectors. If nprobe is raised from 5 to 50 for a query, what's the real effect?
options: Recall moves closer to an exact brute-force scan, at the cost of scanning more vectors and taking longer per query
Query speed improves because fewer clusters need to be built
The collection's distance metric automatically switches from cosine to Euclidean
Nothing changes, because nprobe only affects index build time, not query time
questions.explain: Lesson 12 is explicit about nprobe's trade-off: probing more clusters means recall goes up, closer to what an exact scan would find, but query time goes up too, because more vectors get scanned per search.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the popular vector database landscape, from Lesson 11.
options: Pinecone is fully managed, with no self-hosted or open-source option
Chroma runs embedded inside your own process by default, with no separate server required
Milvus was built from the ground up for small, single-machine deployments only
Qdrant, Weaviate, and Milvus each also offer a managed cloud version of their open-source engine
Which category a database falls into (managed vs. self-hosted) determines which one has mathematically better search quality
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is direct: Pinecone is managed-only with no self-hosted option, Chroma is embedded by default, and Qdrant/Weaviate/Milvus (as Zilliz Cloud) each offer a managed cloud version of their open-source engine. Milvus is actually built for very large, distributed scale, and the managed-vs-self-hosted category describes what you operate, not which one searches better.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a query that runs the nearest-neighbor search first and only afterward discards results that fail a metadata filter is called ________-filtering, and it risks returning fewer results than requested.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 names this exact risk: post-filtering runs the ANN search first, then throws away any result that fails the filter — if the filter is restrictive, you can end up with far fewer results than you asked for even though better matches exist deeper in the collection.

questions.prompt: Match each hybrid-search concept, from Lesson 14, to what it actually does.
right: Embedding-based nearest-neighbor search — strong on meaning, can under-rank exact terms
Term-based search like BM25 — strong on exact matches, misses paraphrase
Scores each result by 1/(k + its rank) in each list it appears in, then sums
Normalizes both score lists to 0-1 and combines them using a tunable weight
questions.explain: Lesson 14 covers dense and sparse search as complementary, then two ways to fuse them: RRF scores by rank position summed across lists, while weighted blending normalizes both scores onto the same scale and combines them with an alpha weight.

questions.prompt: Using Qdrant's published formula (vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes × 1.5), roughly how much RAM does a collection of 2,000,000 vectors at 1,536 dimensions need for its index?
questions.explain: 2,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 bytes × 1.5 ≈ 18,432,000,000 bytes, or about 18.4 GB — twice the 9.2 GB Lesson 15 calculates for 1,000,000 vectors at the same dimensionality, since this collection has twice as many vectors.

questions.prompt: Why does LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter include a chunk_overlap, such as repeating the trailing 50 characters of one chunk at the start of the next?
options: So a sentence that spans a chunk boundary still appears in full in at least one chunk
So the embedding model runs faster on each chunk
So every chunk ends up exactly the same length
So the vector database can skip storing metadata for overlapping chunks
questions.explain: Lesson 16 explains chunk_overlap directly: repeating a trailing slice of one chunk at the start of the next means a sentence that spans a chunk boundary still appears in full at least once, instead of being cut in half and losing meaning.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three chunking strategies from Lesson 16.
options: Fixed-size chunking splits on a raw character or token count with no regard for sentence boundaries
Recursive chunking tries separators in order — paragraph, then sentence, then word — falling back to a harder split only when needed
Semantic chunking costs an embedding call per sentence just to decide where to cut
Fixed-size chunking is the practical default for most RAG pipelines
Semantic chunking is typically the cheapest of the three strategies to run at scale
questions.explain: Lesson 16 names recursive/structure-aware chunking as the practical default, precisely because it respects document structure while guaranteeing a maximum size. Fixed-size ignores structure, and semantic chunking is the most expensive of the three, not the cheapest, because it costs an embedding call per sentence.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: smaller chunks usually need a ________ top_k, because any single chunk carries less context on its own and you need more of them to assemble a full answer.
questions.explain: Lesson 17 ties chunk size and top_k together directly: smaller chunks carry less context each, so retrieval usually needs a higher top_k to gather enough of them to actually answer the question.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a query-time RAG round trip, from Chapter 4, in the correct order.
items: The user's question is embedded with the same model used on the stored chunks
Vector search returns a wider candidate list of top-k chunks, each with a similarity score
A re-ranker scores the query and each candidate together, narrowing and reordering the list
The narrowed, numbered chunks are assembled into a grounded prompt alongside the question
The model generates an answer, citing back to the numbered context
questions.explain: Lessons 18 through 21 build this round trip in exactly this order: embed the question, retrieve a wider candidate set cheaply, re-rank that smaller set more accurately, assemble the narrowed chunks into a grounded, numbered prompt, then generate a cited answer.

questions.prompt: A re-ranker (cross-encoder) is more accurate at judging relevance than vector search alone. Why does it still run on a pre-narrowed candidate list from vector search, rather than on the whole collection directly?
options: Because a cross-encoder scores the query and each chunk jointly, which can't be pre-computed and stored, making it far too expensive to run against millions of chunks
Because re-rankers are physically limited to comparing exactly two documents at a time
Because vector search is always more accurate than a re-ranker, so re-ranking is just a tie-breaker
Because re-ranking requires the candidate chunks to already be translated into a different language
questions.explain: Lesson 19 explains exactly why the order matters: a re-ranker's joint query/chunk scoring is more accurate but can't be pre-computed the way chunk embeddings can, so vector search cheaply narrows millions of chunks down first, and the re-ranker spends its expensive judgment only on that short list.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about citations and handling retrieval failures.
options: A citation is only as good as the metadata — like a source ID and page — the chunk was stored with at ingestion time
The Messages API's built-in Citations feature ties each claim to cited_text structurally, without depending on the model remembering to add bracket numbers
A score_threshold below which no results are returned at all is a way to catch the "nothing relevant exists" failure mode
A fluent, confident-sounding answer is always proof that retrieval actually succeeded
Widening a search by dropping a metadata filter is never an appropriate response to a retrieval failure
questions.explain: Lessons 21 and 22 establish all three true statements directly: citations trace back to ingestion-time metadata, the built-in Citations feature structurally ties claims to sources, and a score_threshold catches the clearest retrieval failure. A confident answer is explicitly not proof of success, and widening a search is listed as one of the honest responses to a failure, not something to avoid.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a pipeline that responds "I don't have information about that" instead of forcing a weak, low-scoring chunk into the prompt is practicing ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 22 names abstention as one of the three honest responses to a detected retrieval failure — saying "I don't know" is always safer than fabricating an answer from context that doesn't actually support it.

questions.prompt: HyDE embeds a fake, unverified hypothetical answer instead of the user's original question. Why does this actually improve retrieval, even though the hypothetical answer's facts might be wrong?
options: Because the hypothetical answer is written in the same answer-style and structure as real stored answer chunks, so its embedding lands closer to the real answer's embedding than a terse question's embedding would — the match is won on style, not on whether the facts are correct
Because the hypothetical answer is fact-checked against the vector database before being embedded
Because HyDE always returns more chunks per query than a standard retrieval call
Because the hypothetical document replaces the need for an embedding model entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 24 is explicit that HyDE's improvement comes from closing a style gap, not a facts gap: a short question and a detailed answer sit in different regions of embedding space, and a hypothetical document written in answer-style lands closer to a real answer chunk even when its specific facts are wrong.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about multi-query RAG and agentic RAG.
options: Multi-query RAG generates several different phrasings of the same question, retrieves separately for each, and deduplicates the combined results by chunk ID
Agentic RAG exposes retrieval as a tool the model can choose to call zero, one, or several times
Multi-query RAG is cheaper per query than a single retrieval pass, because the reformulations reuse the same embedding call
In agentic RAG, the model always retrieves exactly once, the same as a single-pass pipeline
An agentic RAG model can read what a first search returned and issue a second, more targeted search before answering
questions.explain: Lessons 23 and 25 are clear on both patterns: multi-query RAG multiplies retrieval cost (separate embedding calls and searches per reformulation, not a shared one), and agentic RAG makes retrieval a tool the model decides to call — zero, one, or several times, including a refined second search based on what the first one returned.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the query language Neo4j and other graph databases use to traverse nodes and relationships, as in MATCH (a:Company)-[:PARENT]->(p:Company), is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 26 introduces Cypher as the real query language graph databases like Neo4j use to match patterns across nodes and relationships, rather than comparing vector similarity.

questions.prompt: Match each RAG evaluation metric, from Lesson 27, to what a low score on it actually means.
right: Retrieval is pulling in a lot of irrelevant chunks alongside the genuinely relevant ones
Retrieval is missing chunks that should have been found at all
The generated answer adds claims the retrieved context doesn't actually support
The answer is faithful to the retrieved context but doesn't actually address the question asked
questions.explain: Lesson 27 separates these four failure modes deliberately: precision and recall both describe retrieval quality from opposite angles, while faithfulness and answer relevancy both describe generation quality from opposite angles — a pipeline can be weak in any one of these without being weak in the others.

questions.prompt: Why does this course's capstone stay scoped to one knowledge base instead of three different document sets?
options: Because the point is proving every pipeline stage is genuinely wired up — a re-ranker that actually reorders results, a citation that actually points at a real chunk — which a three-source build done halfway would demonstrate far less convincingly
Because vector databases have a hard technical limit of one collection per API key
Because embedding models can only be licensed for a single document source at a time
Because re-ranking APIs charge per knowledge base connected, making more than one prohibitively expensive
questions.explain: Lesson 28 states the reasoning directly: a one-source assistant where every stage actually works teaches more than a three-source assistant where none of those stages are fully working — the capstone's value is in proving the pipeline is real, not in covering more ground.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the capstone's evaluation-and-tuning workflow, from Lesson 30, in the correct order.
items: Build a small evaluation set that includes at least one honest "I don't know" case
Run the pipeline on each test case and record what it actually retrieved and answered
Run Ragas evaluate() against that recorded dataset
Read which specific metric is low to decide which pipeline stage to investigate
Make one measured tuning change and re-run the same evaluation set to confirm it helped
questions.explain: Lesson 30 walks through this exact sequence: build an honest test set first, run the real pipeline against it and record its actual behavior, evaluate that recorded data, use the specific low metric to point at a specific stage, then make one change and re-measure with the same evaluation set to confirm it actually helped.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reading the capstone's evaluation scores, from Lesson 30.
options: Low context_precision points toward checking the score_threshold, or whether chunk size is too large
Low context_recall points toward checking top_k, or whether chunking split a relevant passage apart from the context it needed
Low faithfulness proves retrieval itself is broken, not generation
A tuning change isn't considered done until the same metric that flagged the problem is re-measured and shown to improve
Faithfulness and context recall measure the exact same underlying failure mode, just under two different names
questions.explain: Lesson 30 maps precision to over-broad or noisy retrieval and recall to missed chunks, treats faithfulness as a generation-side problem even with good context in hand, and insists a fix isn't confirmed until the same flagged metric is re-measured — faithfulness and context recall are explicitly two distinct failure modes, not duplicates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the next course in the AI Engineer path, covering a model deciding for itself when to call a tool and holding for human approval on consequential actions, is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 31 names AI Agents as the course that picks up exactly where this one leaves off, moving from a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline to a model that decides for itself when to call a tool, including holding for human approval on consequential actions.
